raw_text:
Since the inception of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), transfemoral access has been established as the gold-standard route due to its lower complication profile and quicker recovery times. However, a significant cohort of patients presenting with severe aortic stenosis are precluded from transfemoral TAVR due to unfavorable aortoiliofemoral anatomy, including severe peripheral arterial disease (PAD), vessel caliber mismatch, or extreme tortuosity. For these patients, alternative minimally invasive access routes are required. Historically, alternative routes required surgical exposure of the chest cavity (e.g., transapical or transaortic access) or surgical cutdown of supra-aortic vessels (e.g., transcarotid or transaxillary/subclavian access) [1]. Transcaval (caval-aortic) access has emerged as a novel, fully percutaneous alternative designed to deliver large-bore devices directly to the abdominal aorta without opening the chest or surgical vessel exposure. Initially conceptualized and validated in preclinical animal models [1], the technique was successfully transitioned to human application with the first successful clinical series published in 2014 [2].

The success of the transcaval approach relies on the unique anatomical proximity of the infrarenal abdominal aorta and the adjacent inferior vena cava (IVC), which are separated only by retroperitoneal connective tissues. Pre-procedural planning is heavily dependent on high-resolution multi-detector computed tomography (CT) to identify a suitable crossing zone [3]. This target crossing window must be free of significant aortic calcification and positioned away from critical vascular structures, such as lumbar arteries, the renal artery bifurcation, or major venous tributaries [4]. Furthermore, the pre-procedural CT scan helps ensure that no abdominal organs, such as bowel loops, are interposed between the aorta and the IVC [5]. Careful CT co-registration is critical to defining the exact trajectory and angle for crossing, thereby preventing iatrogenic injury to surrounding structures [6].

During the procedure, vascular access is secured through both the femoral vein and the contralateral femoral artery. A gooseneck snare is advanced via the arterial system and positioned in the infrarenal aorta at the level of the target crossing window. A microcatheter carrying a 0.014-inch coronary guidewire is advanced through the femoral vein to the IVC, aligned with the snare under orthogonal fluoroscopic guidance. Puncture is achieved by applying electrosurgical energy (electrocautery) to the guidewire, allowing it to easily traverse the venous and aortic walls into the snare, establishing a temporary caval-aortic tract [7]. After the structural intervention is complete, the closing of this tract represents a key stage of the procedure, often requiring temporary occlusion [8]. In cases of resistant aortic walls, transcaval crossing can be completed using laser-assisted techniques [9]. Current clinical consensus outlines standardized methods to secure the crossing pathway [10]. Once snared, the wire is exchanged, and a large-bore introducer sheath is placed from the IVC directly into the aorta, facilitating the intervention [11].

The most counterintuitive aspect of transcaval access is its safety profile. In the event of a persistent channel, retroperitoneal hemorrhage is prevented because the hydrostatic pressure of the retroperitoneum exceeds the venous pressure of the adjacent IVC. Consequently, any aortic blood extravasating through the puncture tract decompresses harmlessly back into the low-pressure venous system, forming a temporary aortocaval shunt rather than an expanding retroperitoneal hematoma. This physiological safety mechanism has been validated in large-scale clinical registries and meta-analyses [12]. Complete hemostasis of the tract is achieved at the end of the procedure using off-label occlusion devices, such as nitinol-based Amplatzer duct occluders (typically ADO-I or ADO-II), or a dedicated transcaval closure device [13]. Long-term follow-up demonstrates excellent safety, with high rates of technical success, spontaneous fistula closure, and minimal long-term sequelae [14].

Clinical outcomes for transcaval access are highly favorable when compared to other non-femoral approaches. The versatility of the transcaval approach has been demonstrated across challenging clinical scenarios, including the successful execution of TAVR in morbidly obese cohorts [15]. Its utility has also expanded to emergency procedures, such as percutaneous mechanical circulatory support via venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) in patients with cardiogenic shock [16]. Beyond structural heart interventions, transcaval access has enabled other large-bore interventions like percutaneous thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) [17], as well as the delivery of high-flow microaxial pumps to support compromised ventricular function [18]. Comparative studies indicate that the clinical efficacy and safety of transcaval access match or exceed other surgical alternatives [19]. Review of alternative accesses underscores that transcaval access serves as a viable percutaneous route [20], providing a reliable pathway for patients with hostile peripheral arterial disease who are otherwise considered "no-option" candidates [21].

As clinical experience with transcaval access has matured, operators have integrated advanced procedural variations and troubleshooting protocols. For instance, in patients with extremely calcified or thick aortic walls, laser-assisted crossing has been successfully utilized to facilitate entry [22]. The technique has also been leveraged for advanced biventricular circulatory support, highlighting its applicability beyond isolated left-sided unloading [23]. Comparative studies have evaluated the intermediate-term outcomes of transcaval access relative to subclavian/axillary accesses, demonstrating non-inferior clinical safety profiles [24]. Furthermore, technological refinements such as intravascular ultrasound (IVUS)-assisted aorta-outward puncture have emerged to increase traversal precision [25]. To ensure safety, operators are encouraged to follow established clinical frameworks, such as the "seven pillars" of transcaval TAVR [26]. Detailed procedural guides and surgical vignettes continue to lower the learning curve for newly established structural programs [27].

Despite its procedural success, transcaval access is not without risks. Abandoned or misaligned crossing attempts can result in iatrogenic pseudoaneurysms or persistent retroperitoneal leaks [28]. Operators must adhere to the principle of "honoring our commitments" to a completed traversal, as partial crossings can fail to decompress into the IVC and instead cause arterial bleeding [29]. Lastly, the applicability of the technique is highly relevant for complex patient profiles, such as patients with bicuspid aortic valves who undergo transcaval interventions [30]. Continuous education, standardized planning, and the development of dedicated, commercially available crossing and closure devices will be key to further expanding this vital alternative access option.
